Compare two tests or rules

Source: R/accuracy.R
compare_tests.Rd

Posterior summaries of the differences in sensitivity, specificity and Youden index (first minus second) and of the ratios of the true and false positive rates (first over second) (Alonzo, 2005; Pepe and Alonzo, 2001; Schatzkin et al., 1987).

Usage

compare_tests(fit, first, second, level = 0.95)

Arguments

fit

A fitted model, from baysesp().

first, second

Two tests (by name) or two rules, see test_rule.

level

Probability of the credible intervals.

Value

A data frame as in test_accuracy(), with the additional column probability: the posterior probability that a difference is positive or that a ratio is greater than 1.

Details

The accuracy is defined for a rule \(R\), which declares a subject positive or negative from the response profile \(t\), the vector of the results of the tests: \(r_R(t) = 1\) if the profile is declared positive, 0 otherwise. A single test is the rule "this test is positive". The quantities depend on the prevalence \(\pi = P(D = 1)\) and on the distribution of the profiles in the diseased, \(\theta_{1,t} = P(T = t \mid D = 1)\), and in the healthy, \(\theta_{0,t} = P(T = t \mid D = 0)\):

  • sensitivity (Se): $$Se_R = P(R \textrm{ positive} \mid D = 1) = \sum_t r_R(t)\, \theta_{1,t},$$ the proportion of diseased subjects that the rule declares positive. It is also called the true positive rate (TPR);

  • specificity (Sp): $$Sp_R = P(R \textrm{ negative} \mid D = 0) = 1 - \sum_t r_R(t)\, \theta_{0,t},$$ the proportion of healthy subjects that the rule declares negative; \(1 - Sp_R\) is the false positive rate (FPR);

  • positive predictive value (PPV): $$PPV_R = P(D = 1 \mid R \textrm{ positive}) = \frac{\pi\, Se_R}{\pi\, Se_R + (1 - \pi)(1 - Sp_R)},$$ the probability that a subject declared positive is diseased;

  • negative predictive value (NPV): $$NPV_R = P(D = 0 \mid R \textrm{ negative}) = \frac{(1 - \pi)\, Sp_R}{(1 - \pi)\, Sp_R + \pi\, (1 - Se_R)},$$ the probability that a subject declared negative is healthy.

Sensitivity and specificity describe the rule and do not depend on the prevalence; the predictive values describe what a result means for a subject, and change with the prevalence of the population. For combined rules, such as any_positive(), the accuracy depends on the joint distribution of the tests, not only on their individual sensitivities and specificities (Torrance-Rynard and Walter, 1997; Vacek, 1985).

Each quantity is computed from every posterior draw of \(\pi\), \(\theta_0\) and \(\theta_1\). The results report its posterior mean and median and an equal-tailed credible interval with probability level.

For two rules \(R\) (first) and \(R'\) (second):

  • differences: \(\Delta Se = Se_R - Se_{R'}\), \(\Delta Sp = Sp_R - Sp_{R'}\) and, for the Youden index \(J_R = Se_R + Sp_R - 1\), which summarises the accuracy in one number (0 for a useless test, 1 for a perfect one), \(\Delta J = \Delta Se + \Delta Sp\). A positive difference favours the first rule;

  • ratios of the true positive rates, \(rTPR = Se_R / Se_{R'}\), and of the false positive rates, \(rFPR = (1 - Sp_R) / (1 - Sp_{R'})\). For example, \(rTPR = 1.2\) means that the first rule detects 20% more diseased subjects; \(rFPR < 1\) means that it gives fewer false positives.

The column probability is the posterior probability that a difference is positive, or that a ratio is greater than 1. \(P(rTPR > 1)\) equals \(P(\Delta Se > 0)\), and \(P(rFPR > 1)\) equals \(P(\Delta Sp < 0)\).

When some profile is never verified, the differences depend on the prior of its proportion of diseased (Gustafson, 2015), but the ratios do not, as long as neither rule declares a never-verified profile positive (Alonzo, 2005; Pepe and Alonzo, 2001; Schatzkin et al., 1987). In that case the signs of the differences in sensitivity and in specificity are also identified, through the probabilities of the ratios.

References

Alonzo, T. A. (2005). Verification bias-corrected estimators of the relative true and false positive rates of two binary screening tests. Statistics in Medicine, 24(3), 403–417. doi:10.1002/sim.1959

Gustafson, P. (2015). Bayesian Inference for Partially Identified Models: Exploring the Limits of Limited Data. Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, FL.

Pepe, M. S. and Alonzo, T. A. (2001). Comparing disease screening tests when true disease status is ascertained only for screen positives. Biostatistics, 2(3), 249–260. doi:10.1093/biostatistics/2.3.249

Schatzkin, A., Connor, R. J., Taylor, P. R. and Bunnag, B. (1987). Comparing new and old screening tests when a reference procedure cannot be performed on all screenees. American Journal of Epidemiology, 125(4), 672–678. doi:10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a114580

Torrance-Rynard, V. L. and Walter, S. D. (1997). Effects of dependent errors in the assessment of diagnostic test performance. Statistics in Medicine, 16(19), 2157–2175. doi:10.1002/(SICI)1097-0258(19971015)16:19<2157::AID-SIM653>3.0.CO;2-X

Vacek, P. M. (1985). The effect of conditional dependence on the evaluation of diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 41(4), 959–968. doi:10.2307/2530967

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(1)
d <- simulate_study(n = 1000, prevalence = 0.2,
                    sensitivity = c(A = 0.9, B = 0.8),
                    specificity = c(A = 0.85, B = 0.95),
                    verification_prob = c(0.2, 0.9, 0.9, 1))
d <- baysesp_data(d, tests = c("A", "B"), verified = "verified", disease = "disease")
fit <- baysesp(d, seed = 1)
compare_tests(fit, "A", "B")
#>                quantity          mean        median       lower       upper
#> 1         Se[A] - Se[B]  0.0972856186  0.0977011712  0.02168599  0.17650180
#> 2         Sp[A] - Sp[B] -0.0977881666 -0.0975503042 -0.12733509 -0.06859078
#> 3 Youden[A] - Youden[B] -0.0005025481 -0.0008030661 -0.08393341  0.08597781
#> 4       TPR[A] / TPR[B]  1.1252383139  1.1232906839  1.02670754  1.23966427
#> 5       FPR[A] / FPR[B]  2.8959639962  2.8492295512  2.05311774  4.02143271
#>   identified probability
#> 1       TRUE      0.9920
#> 2       TRUE      0.0000
#> 3       TRUE      0.4945
#> 4       TRUE      0.9920
#> 5       TRUE      1.0000
compare_tests(fit, any_positive(), "A")
#>                           quantity        mean      median        lower
#> 1         Se[any positive] - Se[A]  0.09423374  0.09274048  0.055726849
#> 2         Sp[any positive] - Sp[A] -0.04595762 -0.04552620 -0.061781377
#> 3 Youden[any positive] - Youden[A]  0.04827612  0.04666800  0.006056152
#> 4       TPR[any positive] / TPR[A]  1.10710037  1.10470621  1.060645167
#> 5       FPR[any positive] / FPR[A]  1.30643854  1.30173813  1.205143968
#>         upper identified probability
#> 1  0.14027900       TRUE     1.00000
#> 2 -0.03222708       TRUE     0.00000
#> 3  0.09702180       TRUE     0.98775
#> 4  1.16696488       TRUE     1.00000
#> 5  1.43132449       TRUE     1.00000
# }
